blocks.text: A carbon-fibre drive shaft transmits the torque of a racing car at under half the mass of a steel shaft. Yet a single sheet of the same carbon-fibre prepreg, pulled across the fibres, is barely stiffer than a plastic. The shaft works because the fibres are laid at carefully chosen angles and stacked in a carefully chosen order: a laminate is designed ply by ply.

blocks.markdown: A **lamina** (ply) is a thin layer of unidirectional fibres in a matrix, with very different properties along and across the fibres. A **laminate** is a stack of plies, each at its own angle $\theta$ to a reference axis $x$. Its in-plane behaviour is controlled by the angles and thicknesses of the plies; its out-of-plane (bending and coupling) behaviour is also controlled by the order in which they are stacked.

blocks.title: Ply axes, angle and stacking notation
blocks.text: The **1-axis** runs along the fibres and the **2-axis** across them. The ply angle $\theta$ is measured from the laminate $x$-axis to the fibre direction. A laminate code lists the plies from the top, in degrees: $[0/90/90/0]$. A subscript s ($[0/45/-45]_s$) means the sequence is repeated in mirror order about the mid-plane, giving $0, 45, -45, -45, 45, 0$.

blocks.caption: Unidirectional carbon/epoxy ply used in the worked examples of this unit.
Modulus of a single unidirectional ply loaded at an angle theta to the fibres. At theta = 0 it equals E1 and at theta = 90 degrees it equals E2.

blocks.prompt: For the CFRP ply in the table, find the modulus $E_x$ when the load axis is at $\theta=30^\circ$ to the fibres, and compare with $E_1$.

Invert to obtain the modulus and compare.

blocks.answer: At 30 degrees the ply has a modulus of only 21.3 GPa, about 15 % of its fibre-direction value; a 30 degree misalignment costs most of the stiffness.

blocks.markdown: **In-plane stiffness of a laminate.** If the plies are thin and the stress is uniform through the thickness, the laminate behaves as the thickness-weighted average of the plies' reduced stiffnesses transformed to the laminate axes. The in-plane stiffness matrix $\mathbf{A}$ therefore depends on the **angles and the fraction of thickness at each angle**, but *not* on the order in which the plies are stacked. Bending stiffness is different: plies far from the mid-plane contribute most, so the stacking sequence strongly affects it.

blocks.caption: Q-bar is the ply stiffness transformed to the laminate axes, t_k the thickness of ply k and h the total thickness. The sum does not depend on the stacking order.

blocks.title: In-plane modulus of a cross-ply laminate
blocks.prompt: A $[0/90]_s$ laminate is made from the CFRP ply (equal thickness plies, half at $0^\circ$ and half at $90^\circ$). Estimate the laminate modulus $E_x$ (a) by simple averaging of $E_1$ and $E_2$, and (b) from the full average of the reduced stiffnesses, given $Q_{11}=140.9$ GPa, $Q_{22}=10.06$ GPa and $Q_{12}=3.02$ GPa.

steps.text: Simple estimate: half the thickness has modulus $E_1$ along $x$ and half has $E_2$.
Full average of the ply stiffnesses along $x$ (the $0^\circ$ ply contributes $Q_{11}$ to $A_{11}$ and the $90^\circ$ ply $Q_{22}$), and the cross term is $Q_{12}$ for both plies.
Apply the plane-stress relation with zero lateral stress, $E_x=\left(A_{11}A_{22}-A_{12}^{2}\right)/(A_{22}h)$.

blocks.answer: The laminate has an in-plane modulus of about 75 GPa along both x and y (the simple average is within 0.5 %); the stacking order does not change it.

blocks.markdown: **Why a symmetric laminate does not warp.** In general, an in-plane load can cause curvature, and a bending moment can cause in-plane strain, through the coupling matrix $\mathbf{B}=\sum\overline{\mathbf{Q}}_k t_k z_k$, where $z_k$ is the distance of ply $k$ from the mid-plane. If the laminate is **symmetric** (every ply above the mid-plane has an identical ply, same material, thickness and angle, at the mirror position below), the contributions of the pairs have the same $\overline{\mathbf{Q}}t$ but opposite $z$, and cancel: $\mathbf{B}=\mathbf{0}$. An in-plane load then produces no curvature, so the laminate stays flat. An unsymmetric laminate such as $[0/90]$ has $\mathbf{B}\ne\mathbf{0}$, and warps both under load and after the heat of curing.

blocks.title: Symmetric versus balanced
blocks.text: **Symmetric** (mirror about the mid-plane) makes $\mathbf{B}=\mathbf{0}$ and prevents bending-extension coupling and cure warping. **Balanced** (every $+\theta$ ply has a matching $-\theta$ ply) makes the shear-extension terms $A_{16}=A_{26}=0$, so a tensile load produces no shear distortion. Good practice uses both.

blocks.markdown: **A tube in torsion.** For a thin-walled tube of mean radius $r$ and wall thickness $t$, a torque $T$ gives a pure shear stress $\tau=T/(2\pi r^{2}t)$. Pure shear is equivalent to a tension $\tau$ at $+45^\circ$ and a compression $\tau$ at $-45^\circ$ to the tube axis. Plies with fibres at $\pm45^\circ$ therefore carry the load along their fibres, which is the stiffest, strongest direction, while a $0^\circ$ ply would carry almost none of the shear. The $[\pm45]$ laminate in the table has a shear modulus of 36 GPa against 5 GPa for a unidirectional ply.

blocks.caption: T is the torque, r the mean radius and t the wall thickness of a thin tube; the principal stresses are tension and compression of magnitude tau at plus and minus 45 degrees to the axis.

points: A ply is much stiffer along the fibres than across them, and its modulus drops rapidly with off-axis angle: 21.3 GPa at 30 degrees for a ply with $E_1=140$ GPa.
In-plane laminate stiffness depends on the ply angles and thickness fractions, not on the stacking order; bending stiffness and coupling do depend on order.
A symmetric laminate has $\mathbf{B}=\mathbf{0}$, so it does not warp under in-plane load; a torsion tube should have its fibres at $\pm45^\circ$, aligned with the principal stresses.

questions.stem: Two laminates are made from the same unidirectional plies, both symmetric: [0/45/-45/90]s and [45/0/90/-45]s. Which statement is correct?

options.text: They have different in-plane stiffness because the outer ply differs
They have the same in-plane and bending stiffness because the plies are the same
They have the same in-plane stiffness but different bending stiffness
They have different in-plane stiffness but the same bending stiffness

questions.correctOptionText: They have the same in-plane stiffness but different bending stiffness

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: the outer ply does not change A, only the distribution of ply positions.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: bending stiffness weights the outer plies more heavily, so the sequence matters.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: the in-plane matrix A depends only on the angles and the thickness fractions, and bending stiffness depends on how far each ply lies from the mid-plane.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: the sequence leaves the in-plane stiffness unchanged, and it is the bending stiffness that differs.

questions.explanation: The in-plane stiffness is a thickness-weighted average of the ply stiffnesses and is independent of order. The bending stiffness involves the square of the distance from the mid-plane, so plies on the outside contribute more, and a different sequence gives a different bending stiffness.

questions.stem: A unidirectional carbon/epoxy ply with $E_1=140$ GPa and $E_2=10$ GPa is loaded along the x-axis. For which fibre angle $\theta$ from the x-axis is the ply modulus $E_x$ smallest?

options.text: $90^\circ$, with fibres perpendicular to the load
$0^\circ$, with fibres along the load
$45^\circ$
All angles give the same modulus

questions.correctOptionText: $90^\circ$, with fibres perpendicular to the load

distractorRationale.a: Correct: loading across the fibres uses the weak matrix-dominated modulus, $E_2=10$ GPa, which is the minimum for this ply.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: the modulus is greatest, equal to $E_1$, with the fibres along the load.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: at 45 degrees the modulus is about 13 GPa, larger than $E_2$.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: a unidirectional ply is strongly anisotropic.

questions.explanation: The off-axis modulus falls from $E_1=140$ GPa at 0 degrees to $E_2=10$ GPa at 90 degrees. For this ply it is about 21 GPa at 30 degrees, 13 GPa at 45 degrees and 10.7 GPa at 60 degrees.

questions.stem: A glass/epoxy ply has $E_1=40$ GPa, $E_2=8$ GPa, $G_{12}=4$ GPa and $\nu_{12}=0.25$. Find its modulus $E_x$ when it is loaded at $60^\circ$ to the fibres, using $1/E_x=\cos^4\theta/E_1+(1/G_{12}-2\nu_{12}/E_1)\sin^2\theta\cos^2\theta+\sin^4\theta/E_2$. Give the answer in GPa.

A $[0/90]_s$ laminate is made from equal-thickness glass/epoxy plies with $E_1=40$ GPa and $E_2=8$ GPa. Estimate the laminate in-plane modulus $E_x$ as the thickness-weighted average of the ply moduli along $x$ (half the thickness at $0^\circ$ and half at $90^\circ$), in GPa.
questions.explanation: Half the thickness is at $0^\circ$ with modulus 40 GPa along $x$ and half is at $90^\circ$ with 8 GPa, so $E_x\approx(40+8)/2=24$ GPa. The full classical lamination calculation, including the Poisson coupling, gives 24.1 GPa, so the average is a close estimate.

questions.stem: Which of the following laminates will warp (curl) when cooled from the cure temperature, or when an in-plane load is applied?

options.text: [0/90]s, a symmetric laminate
[0/45/-45]s, a symmetric laminate
[45/-45/-45/45], a symmetric laminate
[0/90], an unsymmetric laminate

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: the stack 0, 90, 90, 0 is mirrored about the mid-plane, so B = 0.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: the stack 0, 45, -45, -45, 45, 0 is symmetric, so B = 0.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: the stack 45, -45, -45, 45 is mirrored about the mid-plane, so B = 0.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: the plies are not mirrored about the mid-plane, so the coupling matrix B is non-zero.

questions.explanation: A laminate is symmetric if each ply above the mid-plane is repeated at the mirror position below it. Only the laminate whose stack lacks such mirror pairs has bending-extension coupling and therefore curls with temperature change or in-plane load.

questions.stem: Why does a symmetric laminate show no curvature under an in-plane load?

options.text: Because all plies in a symmetric laminate have the same fibre angle
For every ply there is an identical ply at the same distance on the opposite side of the mid-plane, so the coupling terms cancel and B = 0
Because a symmetric laminate has no stiffness in bending
Because the Poisson's ratio of every ply is zero

questions.correctOptionText: For every ply there is an identical ply at the same distance on the opposite side of the mid-plane, so the coupling terms cancel and B = 0

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: symmetric laminates generally contain plies at several angles.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: the coupling terms are weighted by distance from the mid-plane, which is of opposite sign for mirrored plies.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: a symmetric laminate has a well-defined bending stiffness.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: the Poisson's ratio of CFRP plies is non-zero and does not govern warping.

questions.explanation: The coupling matrix is the sum of ply stiffness times thickness times distance from the mid-plane, so contributions from mirrored plies have equal magnitude and opposite sign. With $\mathbf{B}=\mathbf{0}$, in-plane forces produce only in-plane strains.

questions.stem: A thin-walled carbon-fibre tube must carry a pure torque. Which ply arrangement is most effective?

options.text: All plies at 0 degrees to the tube axis
All plies at 90 degrees to the tube axis
A single unidirectional ply wound at 0 degrees with a thicker wall
Plies at plus and minus 45 degrees to the tube axis, aligned with the principal stresses

questions.correctOptionText: Plies at plus and minus 45 degrees to the tube axis, aligned with the principal stresses

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: fibres along the axis carry almost no shear and the matrix would have to resist it.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: hoop fibres are not aligned with the principal stresses in a torsion tube.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: a thicker wall of axial fibres still has the weak shear modulus of the ply, 5 GPa.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: pure shear produces tension and compression at 45 degrees, so fibres there are loaded along their length.

questions.explanation: A torque on a thin tube produces pure shear, which equals a tension and a compression of the same size at 45 degrees. Fibres at $\pm45^\circ$ carry these directly and give a shear modulus of about 36 GPa for the ply used here, against 5 GPa for a unidirectional ply.

questions.stem: A thin-walled composite tube of mean radius 40 mm and wall thickness 2.0 mm carries a torque of 800 N m. Using $\tau=T/(2\pi r^{2}t)$, find the magnitude of the principal stress, in MPa, carried along the fibres of the plus and minus 45 degree plies (take it equal to the shear stress).
questions.explanation: The shear stress is $\tau=800/(2\pi\times0.040^{2}\times0.002)=800/(2.011\times10^{-5})=3.98\times10^{7}$ Pa, or 39.8 MPa. In pure shear the principal stresses have this same magnitude, in tension at $+45^\circ$ and in compression at $-45^\circ$.

questions.stem: Explain how the ply angle and the stacking sequence of a laminate affect its in-plane stiffness. Use the figures for a CFRP ply with $E_1=140$ GPa and $E_2=10$ GPa to illustrate the effect of angle, and say what the stacking sequence changes and what it does not.

In-plane laminate stiffness is the thickness-weighted average of the transformed ply stiffnesses, so it depends on the angles and the fraction of thickness at each angle
Illustrates a laminate example (for example [0/90]s about 75 GPa, quasi-isotropic about 54 GPa, [+45/-45] about 17.7 GPa in Ex)
The order of the plies does not change the in-plane stiffness (matrix A)
The order does change the bending stiffness (D) and the coupling (B), because outer plies contribute most to bending
questions.explanation: In-plane stiffness is controlled by how much material lies at each angle. Stacking order governs behaviour out of plane, so it matters for bending and warping but not for in-plane extension.

questions.stem: Explain why a symmetric laminate does not warp under in-plane loading, and select and justify a layup for a thin-walled tube loaded in torsion. State whether your layup is symmetric and balanced.
markingGuide: Coupling matrix $\mathbf{B}=\sum\overline{\mathbf{Q}}_k t_k z_k$ weights each ply by its distance from the mid-plane
In a symmetric laminate each ply has an identical mirror ply at $-z$, so the contributions cancel and $\mathbf{B}=\mathbf{0}$; in-plane loads then produce no curvature
Torsion produces pure shear, equivalent to tension at +45 degrees and compression at -45 degrees to the axis
Select plies at +45 and -45 degrees (an angle-ply, for example [+45/-45]s), with fibres aligned with the principal stresses; high shear modulus (about 36 GPa for the CFRP ply)
The layup is balanced (equal +45 and -45 plies), preventing shear-extension coupling, and symmetric if mirrored about the mid-plane
May add a few 0 or 90 degree plies for axial or hoop stiffness, if needed
questions.explanation: Mirrored plies cancel each other's coupling terms, so a symmetric laminate remains flat. A tube under torque has tension and compression at 45 degrees, so the efficient layup places its fibres along those directions.
